The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing a proposal to make a non-substantive correction to Exchange Rule 1014, Imposition of Fines for Minor Rule Violations.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Exchange Rule 1014(d)(5) to make a non-substantive correction to the table which describes violations of Rule 520(b). Specifically, the column titled, “Number of Violations Within One Calendar Year,” provides a numerical range of violations which corresponds to the second column which provides the associated sanction. For example, the first row provides that 1 to 5 violations will result in a sanction consisting of a Letter of Caution. Similarly, the second row provides that 6 to 10 violations within one calendar year will result in a sanction consisting of a fine in the amount of $500. The Exchange now proposes to correct the fourth row in the first column to state “16 to 20” whereas it currently incorrectly states “16 or 20.” The Exchange believes this correction will provide clarity and precision in the Exchange's rules and eliminate the potential for confusion regarding violations of Exchange Rule 520(b).
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act [3]
in general, and further the objectives of Section 6(b)(1) of the Act [4]
in particular, in that they are designed to enforce compliance by the Exchange's Members [5]
and persons associated with its Members, with the provisions of the rules of the Exchange. In particular, the Exchange believes that the proposed change will provide greater clarity to Members and the public regarding the Exchange's Rulebook by making a non-substantive correction to rule text. The proposed change will also make it easier for Members to interpret the Exchange's Rulebook.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change also furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act. ( printed page 66767)

The Exchange believes the proposed change promotes just and equitable principles of trade and remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system because the proposed rule change will provide greater clarity to Members and the public regarding the Exchange's Rulebook by making a non-substantive correction to rule text. It is in the public interest for the Exchange's Rulebook to be accurate and concise so as to eliminate the potential for confusion.

and because the rules of the Exchange apply to all Members equally. I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.

1. Purpose

and (iii) make conforming amendments to remove individual product-specific references and update cross-references within the rules.
Background
The Exchange's existing rules permit the listing and trading of options on various types of exchange-traded products, including options on shares of exchange-traded funds (“ETFs”), commodity pool ETFs, currency trust shares, and commodity-based trusts

Specifically, Cboe Options adopted Rules 4.3.06(a)(6) and 4.4.06(c) to establish initial and continued generic listing criteria for options on commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets.[7]
Additionally, Cboe Options amended Rule 4.3.06(a)(4) to remove individual product-specific references for crypto asset ETPs, and in a separate filing [8]
amended Rule 4.3.06(a)(1) to permit the listing of options on ETFs as defined in Rule 6c-11.

The Exchange now proposes to adopt rules that are substantively identical to the Cboe Options Rules described above. Specifically, the Exchange proposes the following amendments.

The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 19.3(i) to establish generic listing criteria for options on commodity-based trusts holding multiple crypto assets. Currently, Rule 19.3(i)(5) permits the listing of options on commodity-based trusts that hold a single crypto asset meeting certain requirements. i. the total global supply of each underlying crypto asset held by the Commodity-Based Trust has an average daily market value of at least $700 million over the last 12 months; and
ii. each crypto asset held by the Commodity-Based Trust underlies a derivatives contract that trades on a market with which the Exchange has a comprehensive surveillance sharing agreement, whether directly or through common membership in the Intermarket Surveillance Group (“ISG”).
These requirements are designed to ensure that each crypto asset underlying options approved for trading on the Exchange has sufficient market capitalization and is subject to adequate market surveillance. These criteria are substantively identical to those approved by the Commission for Cboe Options.[9]

articles.summary: This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is modifying the test of the new electronic informal entry type for merchandise entering the United States through the international mail process to permit transmission of the entry with or without electronic Partner Government Agency (PGA) data.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
                    SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is modifying the test of the new electronic informal entry type for merchandise entering the United States through the international mail process to permit transmission of the entry with or without electronic Partner Government Agency (PGA) data.
                    DATES:
The modification is effective on October 22, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    On June 24, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published a notice in the 
                    Federal Register
                     (91 FR 38007), announcing a test for a new electronic informal entry process for international mail in the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE), the entry type 13 (Informal Mail Entry). The test commenced on September 22, 2026. The new informal entry type 13 is available for international mail shipments valued at $2,500 or less, including those shipments that would previously have been eligible for the 
                    de minimis
                     duty exemption, that are sent to the United States through the international postal network (“international mail”). The Entry Type 13 Test provides an alternative to the interim process for informal mail entries, as set forth in section 145.12(b) of title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations (19 CFR 145.12(b)), and allows filers to file informal entry for qualified international mail shipments electronically in ACE. This test temporarily creates an informal entry pathway for low-value international mail shipments subject to PGA data requirements or duties other than those set forth in Chapters 1-97 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS),[] 
                    
                     which are ineligible for the interim process for informal mail entries, pursuant to 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)-(vi).
                
                    To participate in the test, the importer of record (IOR), who is the owner, purchaser of the merchandise being mailed to the United States, or the licensed broker properly appointed by the owner, purchaser, or consignee, who is acting as an IOR, must file the entry type 13 data required by CBP electronically in ACE. In addition to the above Entry Type 13 Test data elements, merchandise subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the HTSUS, or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, must transmit the additional data mandated by those requirements, as applicable. Participants with shipments subject to PGA data requirements may also transmit PGA data electronically in ACE with their entry type 13 filing. However, CBP is modifying this test to also temporarily accept transmission of an entry type 13 that is not accompanied by complete electronic PGA data, to allow filers to begin using the entry type 13 while they work to ensure that they can electronically submit all of the data required for complete PGA submissions. CBP will announce the conclusion of this temporary acceptance in a future notice published in the 
                    Federal Register
                    . For more information on the test procedures and requirements, please refer to the notice announcing the test (91 FR 38007) and the CBP and Trade Automated Interface Requirements (CATAIR) guidelines for ACE, which may be found at 
                    https://www.cbp.gov/trade/ace/catair.
                    Susan S. Thomas,
Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters on the Brownsville Ship Channel. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with an over-sized dead ship tow transiting the area. Entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector Corpus Christi, or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective without actual notice from October 22, 2026 through October 24, 2026. For the purposes of enforcement, actual notice will be used from October 20, 2026 until October 22, 2026. The rule will be subject to enforcement on only one day during the effective period when the vessel transits from the sea buoy to the International Shipbreaking Limited dock.
If you have questions about this rule, call or email Lieutenant Commander Timothy Cardenas, Sector Corpus Christi Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 800-874-2143, email
Timothy.J.Cardenas@uscg.mil.

II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received notification that International Shipbreaking will be conducting a dead ship towing operation within the Brownsville Ship Channel near Brownsville, TX. This operation will involve the transit of the decommissioned former United States naval vessel USS VICKSBURG from the sea buoy to the International Shipbreaking Limited Dock. Hazards from this operation include but are not limited to obstruction of vessel traffic, navigational limitations, and various other activities which create potential hazards for workers and the public. The Captain of the Port (COTP) Corpus Christi has determined that potential hazards associated with dead ship towing operations are a safety concern for anyone within the work area. Therefore, the COTP is issuing this rule under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, which is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable. The Coast Guard was notified of this event on October 6, 2026, but we must establish this safety zone by October 20, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reason, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a safety zone from October 20, 2026 through October 24, 2026. The safety zone will be enforced on one day during this period. The day and time of enforcement will depend on the weather conditions and the transit of the vessel, and will be announced to the public in advance. The safety zone will cover all navigable waters in the Brownsville Ship Channel within a 500 ft radius of the dead ship tow of the USS VICKSBURG by M/V CAITLIN. Vessels and persons will not be allowed to enter the zone during this time, unless authorized by the Captain of the Port.

SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) is approving Virginia's coal combustion residuals (CCR) permit program under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA). After reviewing the CCR permit program application submitted by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (VADEQ), EPA has determined that Virginia's partial CCR permit program meets the standard for approval under RCRA. Virginia's CCR permit program will operate in lieu of the Federal CCR program with the exception of the specific provisions noted below.

I. General Information
A. Summary of Final Action
EPA is taking final action to approve of Virginia's partial CCR permit program because the Agency finds that the State's program requires each CCR unit in the State to achieve compliance with the minimum requirements in the Federal CCR regulations or with alternative requirements that EPA has determined to be at least as protective as the requirements of the Federal CCR regulations in 40 CFR part 257, subpart D, for the reasons set forth in the Proposed Approval (91 FR 23924, May 4, 2026) and this final action. See, 42 U.S.C. 6945(d)(1)(B).
B. Background
CCR are generated from the combustion of coal, including solid fuels classified as anthracite, bituminous coal, subbituminous coal, and lignite, for the purpose of generating steam to power a generator to produce electricity or electricity and other thermal energy by electric utilities and independent power producers. CCR, commonly known as coal ash, include fly ash, bottom ash, boiler slag, and flue gas desulfurization materials. CCR can be sent offsite for disposal or beneficial use or disposed of in on-site landfills or surface impoundments.
On April 17, 2015, EPA published a final rule creating 40 CFR part 257, subpart D, which established a comprehensive set of minimum Federal requirements for the disposal of CCR in landfills and surface impoundments (80 FR 21302). The rule created a self-implementing program that regulates the location, design, operating criteria, and groundwater monitoring and corrective action for CCR units, as well as the closure and post-closure care of CCR units. It also requires recordkeeping and notifications for CCR units. ACTION:
Inseason modification of 2026-2027 management measures.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces eleven inseason actions for 2026-2027 ocean salmon fisheries. These inseason actions modified the commercial salmon fisheries in the area from United States/Canada border to Cape Falcon, OR.
DATES:
The effective dates for these inseason actions are set out in this
( printed page 66656)
document under the heading “Inseason Actions” and the actions remained in effect until superseded or modified.
The annual management measures for the 2026-2027 ocean salmon fisheries (91 FR 29092, May 19, 2026) govern the commercial and recreational fisheries in the area from the United States/Canada border to the United States/Mexico border, effective from 0001 hours Pacific Daylight Time (PDT), May 16, 2026, until the effective date of the 2027-2028 management measures, which we expect to be May 16, 2027. NMFS is authorized to implement inseason management actions to modify fishing seasons, catch limits, and other management measures considering factors described in regulation (50 CFR 660.409). Inseason actions in the salmon fishery may be taken directly by NMFS (50 CFR 660.409(a)—Fixed inseason management provisions) or upon consultation with the Chairman of the Pacific Fishery Management Council (Council), and the appropriate State Directors (50 CFR 660.409(b)—Flexible inseason management provisions).
Management of the salmon fisheries is divided into two geographic areas: north of Cape Falcon (NOF) (United States/Canada border to Cape Falcon, OR) and south of Cape Falcon (SOF) (Cape Falcon, OR, to the United States/Mexico border). This notice describes inseason actions taken during the 2026-2027 management cycle. These actions affected the NOF commercial salmon fishery, as set out under the heading Inseason Actions below.
Consultation on these inseason actions took place with the Council salmon staff officer and representatives for the appropriate State Directors on May 18, 2026, May 27, 2026, June 3, 2026, June 11, 2026, June 18, 2026, and June 25, 2026. This consultation also included representatives from NMFS, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW), and Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. Representatives from the Salmon Advisory Subpanel and the Salmon Technical Team were also present.
These inseason actions were announced via the NMFS' telephone hotline and U.S. Coast Guard radio broadcast at the time the actions became effective. (50 CFR 660.411(a)(2)).

Inseason Action #1

Inseason action #1 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery from the United States/Canada border to Cape Falcon, OR.

The landing and possession limit in the subareas between the United States/Canada border and the Queets River was 100 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
The landing and possession limit for the subarea between the Queets River and Leadbetter Point was 200 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
The landing and possession limit in the subarea between Leadbetter Point and Cape Falcon was 80 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
Effective dates:
Inseason action #1 went into effect at 12:01 a.m., on May 18, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., May 27, 2026.
Reason and authorization for the action:
Catch rates were lower than anticipated going into the spring season, so increasing the landing and possession limits allowed for more opportunities for fisheries to take advantage of the economic benefit of higher prices early in the season, good fishing, and weather windows. Fishers were allowed to fish up to the subarea limits in multiple subareas, but not exceed the overall NOF landing and possession limit. One limit for the entire NOF area allows for enhanced ability to manage the quota effectively by avoiding fishers catching the full subarea limit in multiple subareas and preventing much higher cumulative catch early in the season. A limit for the entire NOF area and lower limits in certain subareas also ensures fair fishing opportunity throughout the fishery and across ports. The varying limits throughout the smaller subareas allow for greater access to the quota based on the availability of fish in each subarea, which allows for more equitable fishing opportunity and a longer fishing season.

This inseason action modified species caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under 50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii).

on June 24, 2026. We believe the public will benefit from more time to prepare for compliance with these changes.
Christopher Mabelitini, Intellectual Property Rights & E-Commerce Division, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 202-325-6915,
ecommerce@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On June 24, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published an interim final rule in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 37801) implementing in CBP regulations an indefinite suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption under 19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C) for merchandise arriving through the international postal network.[1]
Further, to accommodate the entry of merchandise formerly eligible for the
de minimis
administrative exemption, the interim final rule established a new informal entry process for merchandise valued at $2,500 or less entering the United States through the mail environment, including shipments that would previously have been eligible for the
de minimis
exemption.[2]
The suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption took effect on June 24, 2026. The remainder of the interim final rule was effective on July 24, 2026.
In the interim final rule, CBP made certain shipments ineligible for the new informal entry process for postal shipments. Merchandise subject to Partner Government Agency (PGA) requirements, merchandise subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, are ineligible for the postal informal entry procedures adopted in the interim final rule.[3]
However, in recognition of the time needed for the public to adjust to this formal entry requirement, CBP delayed the compliance date for 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) to October 22, 2026. In consideration of the business process changes necessary to achieve full compliance, CBP provided for a delayed compliance date to allow time for the trade to adjust to the new requirement.
CBP has determined that a further extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network additional time to update their internal systems, develop policies and procedures for submission of relevant data, and to develop the technological infrastructure needed to comply with these requirements. Failure to afford the public extra time to comply with these requirements could lead to disruptions in the flow of important international postal shipments destined to Americans. For this reason, CBP is extending the date for compliance with 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) to January 20, 2027.
II. Administrative Procedure Act
The Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 551et seq.,
generally requires agencies to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
and provide interested persons the opportunity to submit comments prior to issuing a final rule. The APA provides an exception to advance notice and comment requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued) that notice and public comment thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). CBP finds that good cause exists to issue this document as a final rule under the APA's good cause exception, because notice and comment are impracticable.
Providing notice and a public comment period on whether the compliance date should be delayed is impracticable because the current compliance date would have passed within the time needed to permit the solicitation of public comments on this rule. Because the public comment period would overtake the current compliance deadline of October 22, 2026, importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network would still be required to come into compliance with 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) by October 22, 2026. Those importers and other parties who need additional time to comply would not be able to benefit from the extended compliance period that this rule provides.
Additionally, this rule does not impose any new substantive regulatory requirements on any person and merely reflects the extension of the compliance date for 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) as set forth in the interim final rule published on June 24, 2026 (91 FR 37801). An extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers and other parties additional time to update internal systems, revise business practices, and develop technological infrastructure needed to comply with CBP's requirements. Providing immediate certainty that this compliance date is extended is therefore needed to ensure that importers and other parties avoid incurring unnecessary costs, burdens, and other challenges associated with meeting the initial compliance date. AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain General Electric Company (GE) Model CF34-8C1, CF34-8C5, CF34-8C5A1, CF34-8C5A2, CF34-8C5B1, CF34-8E2, CF34-8E2A1, CF34-8E5, CF34-8E5A1, CF34-8E5A2, CF34-8E5A2HA, CF34-8E6, and CF34-8E6A1 engines. This AD was prompted by reports of in-flight “Engine Degraded” messages from the engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS) due to corrosion of the variable geometry (VG) system actuator. This AD requires removing certain electronic engine control (EEC) full authority digital electronic control (FADEC) software versions from service and installing an updated EEC FADEC software that is eligible for installation. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2025-3998; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, any comments received, and other information. The address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Daiyun Fang, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th Street, Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: (206) 910-0063; email:
daiyun.fang@faa.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend 14 CFR part 39 by adding an AD that would apply to certain GE Model CF34-8C1, CF34-8C5, CF34-8C5A1, CF34-8C5A2, CF34-8C5B1, CF34-8E2, CF34-8E2A1, CF34-8E5, CF34-8E5A1, CF34-8E5A2, CF34-8E5A2HA, CF34-8E6, and CF34-8E6A1 engines. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on November 18, 2025 (90 FR 51590). The NPRM was prompted by three separate events involving airplanes with Model GE CF34-8C5 engines installed in which “Engine Degraded” messages were received from the EICAS during flight. A subsequent investigation by the manufacturer revealed that these engines had been operated infrequently over the two-year period prior to these events and stored in close proximity to a saltwater coastline. The investigation further revealed the VG actuation lever arms were stuck due to corrosion between the high-pressure compressor case and vane bushings, which increased the VG actuation loads and slowed the VG response. As a result of this increase, the VG command and actual positions exceeded acceptable disagreement parameters, triggering an EICAS “Engine Degraded” message. In response to the “Engine Degraded” message, the manufacturer and FAA determined that certain versions of the EEC FADEC software installed on GE Model CF34-8E and CF34-8C engines can potentially reduce the engine to idle and lock the throttle until the engine is shut down and restarted. In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require removal of certain EEC FADEC software versions from service and installation of updated EEC FADEC software that is eligible for installation. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Comments
The FAA received comments from three commenters. The commenters were the Airline Pilots Association, International (ALPA), the Citizens Rulemaking Alliance, and Horizon Air. The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Support for the NPRM
ALPA expressed support for the NPRM.
Request To Justify Forgoing Notice and Comment or Issue an NPRM
The Citizens Rulemaking Alliance requested that the FAA place a detailed analysis in the AD docket explaining why prior notice and comment were impracticable for each requirement and why the selected compliance times necessitated immediate issuance. Alternatively, the commenter requested that the FAA either convert this action to an interim final rule limited to actions necessary to mitigate any immediate risk and simultaneously issue an NPRM to solicit comment for 30 to 60 days on non-emergency actions. The commenter asserted the FAA has not adequately justified use of the good cause exception to bypass notice and comment and the 30-day delayed
( printed page 66632)
effective date and must, at a minimum, provide an explanation why a brief comment period was impracticable.
The FAA notes the comment was submitted in response to an NPRM for which the FAA provided a 45-day comment period. This final rule is effective 35 days after its publication in the
Federal Register
. Therefore, the FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Comply With the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
The Citizens Rulemaking Alliance requested that the FAA clarify whether the proposed AD requires reporting. If reporting is required, the commenter requested that the FAA revise the proposed AD to comply with the PRA or suspend the reporting requirement until PRA requirements are satisfied.
The FAA notes that this AD does not require reporting. If an AD were to require reporting, the preamble of the AD would include a paragraph titled “Paperwork Reduction Act” that would provide the applicable OMB control number, required PRA statements, and the estimated time to collect the required information (burden). Any costs associated with the reporting requirement would be included in the Costs of Compliance section in the preamble of the AD. Therefore, the FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.

The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. This action revokes Class E airspace at Diamond “O” Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. This action supports the instrument procedures being cancelled and the decommissioning of the Santa Elena radio beacon (RBN).

Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it removes Class E airspace at the affected airport because it is no longer needed to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9901 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 53203; August 17, 2026) proposing to remove Class E airspace at Diamond “O” Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. No comments were received.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action modifies 14 CFR part 71 by removing the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Diamond “O” Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. This action is the result of instrument procedures being cancelled and the decommissioning of the Santa Elena RBN.

Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
